neutral_facts.value: The prosecution case is that the deceased had constructed some shop on his land. The accused persons demanded Rs. 40,000 from the deceased towards 'Tola Mastani Salami' for the construction of the shops. The deceased refused to succumb to the demand and therefore, the accused threatened to murder him. On the day of the incident, at 9.00 P.M., the deceased had gone to one place in respect of his business, on a bicycle. From there, he returned to his house at 10.00 P.M. On the way, he was restrained by the accused. The accused killed him by strangulation. Thereafter, they cut the body into pieces with a sharp cutting weapon and after putting the same in gunny bags, carried them in a van in the night of the following day and left the same at some place. A witness saw those gunny bags and reported the matter to the police. FIR was lodged and case was registered under s. 302/201/341 IPC against unknown miscreants. The van was recovered on the basis of the driver's statement. All the accused were arrested on different dates. The cycle used by the deceased was recovered. The accused were charged under s. 302, 201, 379, 411 rlw. s. 34 IPC. The prosecution has proved the complete chain of events, including the last seen together theory, the strangulation of the deceased by the accused, and the disposal of the body in gunny bags into a van. The accused absconded immediately after the incident, which supports the prosecution case.

defence_argument.value: The appellants contended that the case was based on circumstantial evidence without a complete chain of events, that the prosecution case was not reliable due to hostile witnesses, that the accused were not named in the FIR, and that s. 34 IPC was not attracted as there was no common intention and participation by all the accused.

quotes.text: The appellants interalia contended that the present case, being a case of circumstantial evidence, does not complete chain of events; that the prosecution case was not reliable because PWs 13 and 23 turned hostile; that the crucial witnesses PWs 8, 17 and 19 did not name the appellant-accused 'SH'; that there was delay in recording evidence of the witnesses; that conviction could not be based on the evidence of related witnesses; that the accused were not named in the FIR; that the appellant-accused was not identified in Tl Parade; and therefore, conviction was not justified. They also contended that s. 34 IPC is not attracted as there was no common intention and participation by all the accused.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle of 'common intention' under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, emphasizing that for the applicability of this provision, two factors must be established: common intention and participation in the crime. The court also emphasized that the common intention may develop at the spur of the moment between a number of persons based on the facts of the case.

quotes.text: For applicability of this provision, two factors must be established i.e. common intention and participation in crime. The provision involves vicarious liability for the act of others. On facts, ingredients of presence of more than two persons, existence of common intention and commission of an overt act stand established.
